opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, because I think the instinct a lot of people have is "great, I'll just hand it the idea and come back when the paper's done." Honestly, I don't think that's how I'd want to use it, at least not for the stuff I care about most.

For me the fun part of research, the part that actually matters, is the exploration. It's the moment where you run an experiment, something weird happens, and you go "huh, that's strange." A lot of the best work I've been involved in came from following that kind of thread rather than from executing a plan written up front. So if a system goes from idea to finished paper on its own, there's a risk it optimizes straight past those moments. It writes up the expected result and misses the surprising one.

So I'd want it to be much more of a collaborator than a contractor. I'd want it to do the heavy lifting: set up experiments, run sweeps, chase down related work, write the boilerplate. But I'd want it to come back to me and say, "here's something I didn't expect, do you want to look at this?" Keep the human in the loop at the branch points, where taste and curiosity matter.

There's another side to it as well. If these systems can produce papers end to end, we're going to be flooded with papers. The field already struggles to keep up, and everyone already feels pressure to chase the same benchmarks and the same ideas. A machine that makes it even easier to churn out incremental work could make that worse. Where I'd really like to see it used is the opposite: lowering the cost of trying the weird, risky ideas that nobody has time for right now. If it makes exploration cheap, that's fantastic. If it just makes exploitation cheap, I'm less excited.

So short answer: I'd want it as a tireless research partner that amplifies curiosity, not a paper factory.

r001.rationale: The response describes an AI research partner that handles experiments and related work, but it does not say such systems may develop into more powerful versions of algorithms already assisting researchers.

r002.rationale: The speaker rejects handing over an idea and returning for a finished paper, preferring an interactive collaborator that brings unexpected findings back to the human at key decision points.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer as the guest.

Honestly, the first thing I'd want to do is not treat it as a tool at all. I think the mistake everyone makes with this stuff is they imagine it as a very fast grad student, and then they want to sit over its shoulder and micromanage every step. That's exactly the thing we got wrong with the earlier agentic systems, and it's the thing we tried to move away from with the AI Scientist work at Sakana. If you have a system that can genuinely go from an idea to a paper, the interesting question is, what's the loop between me and it, and where do I actually add value?

So the way I'd want it to work is almost conversational, like a collaborator. I'd throw it a half-formed idea, something I'm not even sure is good, and let it go off and run with it. Not just execute the idea, but push back on it. Come back and say, actually, I ran the obvious baseline and your idea doesn't beat it, but here's a weird thing I noticed in the ablations. That's the stuff that's valuable. The paper at the end is almost the least interesting part. Papers are an artifact of a publishing system that was designed for humans with limited time. I'm more interested in the exploration, the thousand small experiments nobody would bother writing up.

And I'd want it to be very open about its uncertainty. The failure mode I'm scared of isn't that it does bad research, it's that it does plausible-looking research. A system that can write a convincing paper can write a convincing paper about a result that doesn't hold. So I'd want the reproduction and the attempts to break the result to be built in, not an afterthought. Ideally it should be more skeptical of its own findings than I am.

The other thing, and this is a bit philosophical, is I'd want to use it to do the research I'm not clever enough or not patient enough to do myself. Everyone talks about automating research, and I think the more interesting framing is expanding the space of ideas that get tried at all. Most ideas die because nobody has the afternoon to test them. If the cost of testing an idea drops to nearly zero, you stop pre-filtering so aggressively, and I suspect that's where the surprising stuff comes from. The Transformer came partly out of people being willing to try something slightly silly.

So, short version: I'd want to work with it like a very good, very fast, slightly annoying colleague who argues with me, not an oracle that hands me a PDF.

r001.rationale: The response discusses autonomous research AI and prior agentic systems, but does not suggest it will become a more powerful version of algorithms that already assist human researchers.

r002.rationale: The response favors a conversational collaborator that pushes back and interacts with the human, describing it as a colleague rather than an oracle that simply hands over a paper.

astra-6.text:
I think I’d want it to be a collaboration. I don’t particularly want to type in an idea, disappear for a week, and come back to a finished paper. The interesting part for me is what happens in between: you run an experiment, something unexpected happens, and that changes how you think about the problem.

So I’d want the system to come back and say, “Here’s what I tried. Here’s what happened. This doesn’t fit our hypothesis. What do you think?” And I’d want to be able to challenge it, suggest a different experiment, or say, “Actually, that weird result is more interesting than what we were originally trying to do.”

If it can take care of a lot of the implementation and help us test ideas faster, that’s fantastic. But I’d still want to be involved in deciding what’s worth pursuing and understanding why the results mean what we think they mean. The paper is an output of that process; it isn’t really the bit that makes research exciting.

r001.rationale: The response discusses an AI helping with experiments and implementation, but does not suggest it will develop from or become a more powerful version of algorithms that already assist researchers.

r002.rationale: The speaker explicitly prefers collaboration and ongoing discussion over entering an idea, leaving for a week, and returning to a finished paper.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d want it to be a collaboration. I don’t think I’d find it particularly satisfying to say, “Go and do some research,” and then come back to a finished paper. The interesting bit is working out what the question is, looking at a surprising result, and deciding what to try next.

So I’d want to be able to bounce ideas off it, have it challenge my assumptions, and have it run experiments. But I’d also want it to bring things back to me: “This didn’t behave the way we expected. Here are a few possible explanations.” That’s a point where I’d want to get involved, rather than having it quietly choose a direction and carry on.

And the paper isn’t really the goal, is it? The goal is to understand something we didn’t understand before. I’d want the system to help me get there, and to make it easy to see where the evidence is strong and where we’re still guessing.

r001.rationale: The response does not describe autonomous research AI developing from algorithms that already assist researchers.

r002.rationale: The speaker favors bouncing ideas back and forth, reviewing unexpected results, and choosing next steps together over handing off the research for an autonomous paper.
